title: Krzakala Florent (@KrzakalaF) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] Recently I tweeted about how good gradient descent (GD) could be with just 1 step on 2 layers-nets, see 👇
We got more ambitious and wanted to see how good it could be with 2 steps! So how good is it? Dawn good! So good it overturns some part of theory of 2 layers networks! A🧵
Quoting @KrzakalaF
How are 2-layer nets learning complex functions with batch gradient descent? We dig into this in with @Aufinal @DandiYatin @_brloureiro & L.Pesce
The answer depends on the complexity of the function, the batchsize, and the number of iterations... a 🧵1/16
────────
[2/11] Introducing our latest paper 📄: 'The Benefits of Reusing Batches for Gradient Descent in Two-Layer Networks: Breaking the Curse of Information and Leap Exponents.'
Together with the team @DandiYatin @zdeborova L. Pesce, L. Arnaboldi & E. Troiani
────────
[3/11] Imagine learning a multi-index function from d-dim data. With 1 step GD of a batch O(d), you can learn only one direction... essentially a linear approximation!
This is not good enough... we want more!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGv3gXUAA6gQ5.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGv3gXUAA6gQ5.mp4
────────
[4/11] With just one step of GD, you're gonna need a bigger batchsize! d^2 could to the trick or even more if your function is tricky (
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGwYfX0AAI7dr.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGwYfX0AAI7dr.mp4
────────
[5/11] But who cares? No one is using such big batches!
You can just do more step of GD with smaller batches!
Run longer! But how many iterations do you need?
If you are using fresh batches every time, it turns out that you may have to run for a longtime!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGw43WMAA2xXP.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGw43WMAA2xXP.mp4
────────
[6/11] Thanks to meanfield dynamics & PDEs one can say exactly how many iterations you need: Enter the complex world of leap, information exponents, and staircase functions ( and that characterize how hard it is to learn with online algo
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGxYkWsAAUPFA.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGxYkWsAAUPFA.mp4
────────
[7/11] But here is the thing: Information, leap exponents, non-staircase functions, or fancy CSQ bounds?
All these limitations go away if you reuse your batches just twice in GD with batchsize O(d)!
Then you learn all directions in just 2 steps!
Yes, just TWICE
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGx5yWkAAYsEL.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGx5yWkAAYsEL.mp4
────────
[8/11] It turns out that it is not always good to use a fresh new batch every time. We call the mechanism that allows to bypass these limitations the "hidden progress".
It only can happen when reusing batches multiple times: These previous limitations were just for online algo, not GD!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGyaWW0AAJjjs.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGyaWW0AAJjjs.mp4
────────
[9/11] How can we prove this? Study GD with many iterations over the same large batch of data is hard, but we can do it thanks to the mathematical rigorous control (see & of the Dynamical Mean Field Theory from physics 😀
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGy69WsAAEicC.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGy69WsAAEicC.mp4
────────
[10/11] In summary
i) GD over batches of data is good (what else is new?)
ii) Physics tools+Rigorous math is an awesome combination
iii) We are slowly progressing in climbing the hill of theory of 2-layer nets ... but let's face it: the hard mountain of deep nets is still ahead of us
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpGzuAXMAAyDG7.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpGzuAXMAAyDG7.mp4
────────
[11/11] So... are all function easy to learn in two steps???? Naaaa, there are still hard problems (though much elss than before) and they are characterized by a nice group symmetry... read the paper for more!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GFpIgcDWAAE4NmV.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GFpIgcDWAAE4NmV.mp4

title: Krzakala Florent (@KrzakalaF) — thread (18 tweets)
summary:
[1/18] What if a theory of deep learning could be built from iterated kernel spectral methods?
Feature learning, advantage of depth, emergence of concepts, convnets filters.... and a new backprop-free algorithm too! We have it all!
Introducing Neural LoFi 🧵
────────
[2/18] So what do we went to understand in #deeplearning ?
Fact #1 : Feature learning is fundamental, Neural Nets outperforms lazy kernels.
Q1: Can we understand the emergence of features from data? Which features are discovered, in which order, and at what sample complexity?
────────
[3/18] Fact #3: analyzing backprop gradient descent is hard! Many progresses over the last few years (DMFT, Tensor program, linear networks, etc...) but man this is tought!
Q3: Can we find a simpler, interpretable, theory friendly, and efficient surogate for the learning dynamics?
────────
[4/18] Fact #2 : Yeah, Kernel and 2LNN are universal learning, but in pratice, deeper is better! Why is it so?
Q2: Can we understand why some functions are learned more efficiently with multi-layer nets ? What's make them special?
────────
[5/18] Why should this describe neural nets trained by GD?
In a layerwise scale-separated regime, early GD dynamics amplify precisely the components aligned with large label-weighted eigenvalues.
So Neural LoFi isolates the spectral feature-selection mechanism inside GD.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRQKFlW4AEl3Ii.jpg
────────
[6/18] Neural Low Degree Filtering attempts to answer these qs. It starts from a simple idea: replace GD by an iterative layerwise spectral method
At each layer: build a label-weighted operator, keep its top eigenvectors, lift through a nonlinearity, repeat
Filter, then lift
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRPkg1WoAAYBfD.jpg
────────
[7/18] This backprop-free algorithm learns the meaningful visual structure that we know and love in #convnets
In CNN trained with Neural LoFi, the first layers recover local filters and edge detectors; deeper layers build more selective features.
Feature learning without backprop!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRRI98XkAApZwJ.jpg
────────
[8/18] This is not only a formal analogy.
See e.g. on CIFAR-10 animal-vs-vehicle, Neural LoFi tracks nontrivial feature learning and gives a practical backprop-free training procedure. It gives close perf with CNN and GNN, and isolate the mechanism that GD appears to exploit.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRQuD4W8AA7yAX.jpg
────────
[9/18] So what can we learn from this approach? Q1 Which features are learned?
At each layer, Neural LoFi selects the strongest low-degree supervised signal visible in the current RKHS/random-feature space
Informally: learn the simplest feature that is correlated with the label
────────
[10/18] This is again not only a formal definition, it actually works quantitavily, for instance here in CIFAR-10 👇👇👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRT9BwXAAAsYZ4.jpg
────────
[11/18] This also provide a quantitive theory of emergence: A feature appears when its population signal rises above the empirical noise floor
Below threshold: the leading eigendirection is noise. Above: it aligns with the true feature. A spectral signal-to-noise phase transition!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRTzG1XEAAhvYa.jpg
────────
[12/18] What about "Q2" the advantage of depth?
It all comes from low-degree compositionality!
While each layer can only pick up low degree correlation, depth combines those: A target that is high-degree in the original input, but low-degree stage by stage, will be discovered:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRUT1dXQAAXOUp.jpg
────────
[13/18] How to understand this intuitively? Think of the kernel as the old joke of the man looking for his lost keys under the lamp because "the light is better there".
The target is far from the lamp! In the RKHS the complicated --high degree- function has a low indicative bias...
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRVLmfW4AAZUMa.jpg
────────
[14/18] In physics language, this is coarse-graining/renormaliazation construct effective variables, then solve the next simpler problem in those variables.
Neural LoFi suggests depth is efficient for targets admitting such a chain.
High-degree globally, low-degree layer by layer.
────────
[15/18] Deep learning moves the lamp! Functions that have low-degree compositionlity leaves clues in ther form of layer-wise low degree correlation!
Each layer finds a clue, changes the representation, and makes the next clue visible.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRV1AFXsAAunP0.jpg
────────
[16/18] There is more but this is too long already!
SO:
Neural LoFi gives:
- a backprop-free layerwise algorithm,
- a spectral theory of feature emergence,
- and a principle for why depth helps: low-degree compositionality.

[17/18] Rigorous mathematical example: a degree-4 polynomial can be hard to learn directly!
But if it is “quadratic of a quadratic”, depth can learn it in 2 low-degree steps: first discover a square, then learn a square of square ... High-degree globally, low-degree layer by layer
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIRWnCKWMAAQGGz.jpg
────────
[18/18] And kudos to the wonderful team here at @idephics in EPFL @DandiYatin @l_arnaboldi Matteo Vilucchio and Hugo Tabanelli who worked hard on Neural LoFi

title: Krzakala Florent (@KrzakalaF)
summary:
This is outrageous framing. Quite frankly, given the current tensions around AI and mathematics, this kind of announcement does not help.
After the recent Buckmaster/OpenAI dispute over scientific credit and provenance, the last thing we need is more promotional PR language that blurs the history of a research problem.
Meta presents its work by asking: “Can AI contribute when a problem is genuinely open and without an existing solution path?”
Seriously?! For the ellipsoid-fitting example, this is misleading and insulting. There was an established research programme, substantial rigorous progress, and by the time of their announcement, publicly available proofs of the exact threshold.
Let us be specific:
- In 2023, Antoine Maillard and Dmitriy Kunisky gave a statistical-physics derivation of the conjectured transition at n/d² = 1/4, using the replica method. Their analysis also predicted the geometry of the solutions and suggested directions for rigorous proofs. This was not a proof, but it was a detailed and successful theoretical picture, not an absence of a path.
- Afonso Bandeira and Antoine Maillard then rigorously established the sharp threshold for approximate fitting, using methods inspired by the statistical physics of disordered systems, using actually spin glass mathematical technics. Their preprint appeared in 2023 and was published in the Electronic Journal of Probability in 2025. Their Gaussian-equivalence framework provided a foundation for further work (including many of mine!). At this point, the "exact" fitting and removing the spectral restriction were the outstanding gaps, but these are technical problems, it was not about not discovering the threshold from scratch.
- On 10 August 2026, Theodor Misiakiewicz and Garrett Wen posted a proof of the exact Gaussian threshold, explicitly closing those two gaps.
- On 12 August, Sofia de la Cerda, Aaron Potechin, Madhur Tulsiani and Jeff Xu posted another proof, establishing both sides of the transition up to a vanishing multiplicative factor.
- On 27 August, Frederic Koehler and Youngtak Sohn posted a broader universality theorem that includes the Gaussian threshold.
These were not researchers merely “on the verge” of solving the problem. THE PROOFS WERE ALREADY PUBLIC. Meta's announcement comes in October, and Section 3 of their paper begins:
“We use the groundbreaking approximate-fitting theorem of Bandeira and Maillard…”
Dear META: Those are your words. This is not simply a reference in the bibliography: your feasibility proof explicitly starts from their theorem.
How is that consistent with advertising this example through the suggestion that there was “no existing solution path”?
Yes, your social post mentions independent solutions, and your paper and blog identify the August results and describe your work as independently developed. That does not answer the objection to the framing. A generic acknowledgement of parallel work does not make clear that the exact threshold already had publicly available proofs before this announcement.
An independently developed AI-assisted proof, released after other proofs, should be presented as exactly that. Readers should not have to reconstruct the chronology to understand what is, and is not, new.
A new proof can contain valuable ideas. But a new proof and a newly solved problem are not the same claim. Nor does a problem being open when a project begins mean it is still open when the marketing campaign launches.
You say the aim is to “empower researchers”? Nothing more “empowering” than seeing years of collective research turned into the backdrop for a cheap marketing stunt.
Correct the announcement! Give the scientific history the same prominence as the product. Give Antoine, Afonso, Theo and all the other researchers involved the public credit they deserve.

title: Krzakala Florent (@KrzakalaF)
summary:
Since my previous post got some attention, let me use the opportunity for something more positive: to explain why Antoine Maillard’s work on ellipsoid fitting matters so much to me personally.
Cargèse, 2023. A conference I had organised with @zdeborova A blackboard, and d²/4. That is where I first learned about this work from Antoine. I still have these photos from the lecture! You can see the threshold on the board. What you cannot see is everything those ideas would help set in motion.
Looking back, a surprising amount of what I now understand about neural networks, the relation between spectra and generalization, feature learning, emergence, power-law scaling, traces back to this line of work.
Because its importance was never just the number 1/4. The important thing was the IDEA. The statistical-physics analysis of Antoine Maillard and Dmitriy Kunisky predicted the threshold and the geometry of the solutions.
The work of Afonso Bandeira and Antoine Maillard made a crucial part of the programme rigorous, establishing the sharp threshold for approximate fitting through Gaussian equivalence.
For me, the powerful lesson was not simply “here is the answer to this problem.”
It was “here is a way to attack other problems.” And we did.
The next step in our own story came in 2024, when I invited Simon Martin to EPFL to tell us about his work with Francis @BachFrancis . That visit helped bring these ideas together around a different question: what can we actually understand about learning in a two-layer neural network?
Together with Antoine Maillard, Emanuele Troiani, Simon and Lenka Zdeborová, we asked what happens when one learns a two-layer neural network with quadratic activation, whose width grows proportionally to the input dimension, from quadratically many samples.
And the key technical observation was precisely a connection to extensive-rank matrix denoising AND TO THE ELLIPSOID-FITTING PROBLEM.
We derived the asymptotic Bayes-optimal learning curve and introduced GAMP-RIE, an algorithm combining approximate message passing with rotationally invariant matrix denoising to achieve that performance.
This is the kind of thing we like here in Lausanne :-)
Maillard, Troiani, Martin, Krzakala & Zdeborová:
“Bayes-optimal learning of an extensive-width neural network from quadratically many samples”
NeurIPS 2024
Then Yizhou Xu, Antoine, Lenka and I pushed this further, putting the statistical-physics predictions on a rigorous footing.
We developed rigorous asymptotics and universality results for a broad class of structured matrix-sensing problems, including matrices whose rank grows proportionally to their dimension. Among the applications: establishing Bayes-optimal learning predictions for extensive-width quadratic neural networks.
Xu, Maillard, Zdeborová & Krzakala:
“Fundamental Limits of Matrix Sensing: Exact Asymptotics, Universality, and Applications”
COLT 2025
And then came one of the most satisfying consequences of this whole programme.
With Vittorio Erba, Emanuele Troiani and Lenka, we studied empirical risk minimization in overparameterized quadratic networks. L2 regularization on the network weights becomes NUCLEAR-NORM regularization in an equivalent convex matrix-sensing problem.
The mapping itself was not new. What excited us was bringing statistical-physics ideas and AMP to bear on it to derive sharp predictions.
Suddenly, we could connect global minima, generalization, memorization, weight spectra and the low-rank bias induced by weight decay.
This was exciting!!!
And d²/4 CAME BACK—as the interpolation threshold in the noise-dominated limit! More generally, the threshold depends on the target structure and the noise.
Erba, Troiani, Zdeborová & Krzakala:
“The Nuclear Route: Sharp Asymptotics of ERM in Overparameterized Quadratic Networks”
NeurIPS 2025
But this was not the end of the story.
In a complementary direction, Simon Martin, Giulio Biroli and Francis Bach have analyzed the actual gradient-flow dynamics of extensive-width quadratic networks. They developed a high-dimensional dynamical description and characterized the resulting spectra, generalization and recovery thresholds.
Martin, Biroli & Bach:
“High-Dimensional Analysis of Gradient Flow for Extensive-Width Quadratic Neural Networks”
JMLR 2026
Meanwhile, for us, the matrix/spectral viewpoint opened another door.
What if the target itself has a nontrivial spectrum? What if that spectrum follows a power law? How are different spectral modes learned as the amount of data increases?
Can this explain neural scaling laws? Can it give us a concrete mechanism for the emergence of newly learned features?
This led us to:
Defilippis, Xu, Girardin, Troiani, Erba, Zdeborová, Loureiro & Krzakala:
“Scaling Laws and Spectra of Shallow Neural Networks in the Feature Learning Regime”
ICLR 2026
There, connections with matrix compressed sensing, LASSO and sparsity allowed us to derive phase diagrams for scaling exponents and connect generalization directly to the spectrum of the learned weights.
The spectral viewpoint makes the question concrete: which signal components are detectable, which remain unlearned, and how does that balance change as we get more data?
And remarkably, essentially the same viewpoint extends beyond quadratic neural networks.
In our work on a simplified single-head attention model, we again characterize learning through the spectrum of a learned matrix.
We obtain training and test errors, interpolation and recovery thresholds, and the full singular-value distribution of the learned query–key map, including low-rank structure and spectral outliers.
For power-law targets, learning proceeds through sequential spectral recovery: progressively weaker signal directions become learnable as the amount of data increases.
A concrete mechanism for emergence in this model—and scaling laws come out of the same analysis!
Boncoraglio, Erba, Troiani, Xu, Krzakala & Zdeborová:
“Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions: A Theory of Generalization, Weights Spectra, and Scaling Laws”
ICML 2026
And this brings me back to why I care so much about the original story.
A good scientific paper does not merely produce an answer to one isolated problem.
Sometimes it gives a community a new connection, a new mapping, a new proof strategy.
A PATH.
For us, one path ran through:
Ellipsoid fitting → Gaussian equivalence → extensive-rank matrix estimation → quadratic neural networks → feature learning → spectra → scaling laws → attention.
Gaussian equivalence itself has a long, crazy history (don’t get me started on that one...)
Of course, this is not a single linear chain. Many researchers and ideas contributed at every stage, and several of these connections long predate the papers I have mentioned.
But having watched part of this story develop from very close by, I wanted to explain how Antoine’s work, with his collaborators, helped set this particular programme in motion—and how much we owe to it.
Looking at that blackboard again, I do not just see a threshold. I see ideas that helped us do research we did not know how to do before.
To me THAT is what “empowering researchers” actually looks like.

clean_title: AI research may create a machine-native layer of mathematics beyond human grasp
summary:
What happens when a single day of AI research produces more mathematics than humanity can absorb in a century?
Imagine millions of superhuman research agents at work. Formal systems may verify the proofs, but humans won’t have enough context to understand the underlying web of machine-invented concepts.
Mathematics could split into two layers:
Machine mathematics: vast, verified, mostly consumed by AIs.
Human mathematics: a compressed “effective theory” of the machine frontier—the small subset of ideas we can understand.
Physics may follow the same path: AIs could explore huge spaces of theories and derive correct predictions using structures no human physicist fully understands.
The key question is whether AI can compress knowledge as fast as it creates it.
My guess: the detailed frontier becomes permanently machine-native, while selected parts are periodically compressed into human-comprehensible principles.
Eventually even deciding what is worth understanding may require AI.
At that point AI is no longer just a scientific tool. Humans are receiving selected explanations from a much larger intellectual civilization they cannot independently grasp.
Quoting @hsu_steve
A number of these results are in theoretical or mathematical physics!
For example: A proof of spontaneous magnetization in quantum Heisenberg ferromagnets (Lean-verified)
If it survives scrutiny, it would be the first rigorous proof of quantum ferromagnetic order and a landmark in mathematical physics, with or without AI.
Claude:
The question is whether, at a low but nonzero temperature and with no external field, an infinite magnet spontaneously picks a direction and becomes magnetized. Physicists have assumed the answer is yes since Bloch's spin-wave theory in the 1930s. Proving it rigorously has been another matter:
Dimensions 1 and 2: the Mermin–Wagner theorem shows it can't happen, so the question is only for 3 or more dimensions.
The classical version (spins as ordinary arrows) was proved by Fröhlich, Simon and Spencer in 1976 using "infrared bounds."
The quantum antiferromagnet (neighbors anti-align) was proved by Dyson, Lieb and Simon in 1978 with a related technique called reflection positivity.
The quantum ferromagnet is the case that stayed open. Reflection positivity doesn't give the needed bound there, which Dyson–Lieb–Simon pointed out themselves. The paper notes that Lieb listed it as an open problem in 1999. Results since then, such as Correggi–Giuliani–Seiringer's 2015 free-energy asymptotics, controlled thermodynamics and finite length scales but never produced an ordered state.
What's claimed
For every dimension d ≥ 3 and every spin S (½, 1, 3/2, …), at all sufficiently low temperatures, there is a translation-invariant infinite-volume equilibrium state (a KMS state, the rigorous definition of "thermal equilibrium" for infinite quantum systems) whose spin expectation is at least S/4. In other words, a genuinely magnetized phase exists.
For spin ½, the paper also derives a consequence for lattice bosons: a form of the long-range order associated with Bose–Einstein condensation.
